name: Audio and Video Evidence
title: Audio and Video Evidence
answer: Audio and video evidence in e-discovery covers any recorded sound or moving image that may be relevant to a legal matter, including voicemail, call recordings, body camera footage, surveillance video, deposition recordings, and social media clips. It is a subset of electronically stored information, so it follows the same discovery lifecycle from identification and collection through processing, review, and production. The scope also includes the metadata that travels with the media, such as timestamps, device identifiers, and geolocation, plus any transcripts or captions generated from the content. Because these files are often large and unstructured, they require specialized handling that differs from text documents.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Audio and video evidence in e-discovery covers any recorded sound or moving image that may be relevant to a legal matter, including voicemail, call recordings, body camera footage, surveillance video, deposition recordings, and social media clips. It is a subset of electronically stored information, so it follows the same discovery lifecycle from identification and collection through processing, review, and production. The scope also includes the metadata that travels with the media, such as timestamps, device identifiers, and geolocation, plus any transcripts or captions generated from the content. Because these files are often large and unstructured, they require specialized handling that differs from text documents.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure for audio and video evidence runs on scalable storage and compute, often in a cloud environment, because a single hour of video can consume several gigabytes. Processing pipelines use media frameworks to decode formats like MP4, WAV, and MOV, then split audio from video for separate analysis. Speech recognition engines convert audio to text, while video analysis may sample frames for object detection or optical character recognition. Chain of custody systems record hash values and audit logs at every step, and review platforms index the resulting transcripts and metadata for search.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with ingestion, where files are hashed and their metadata is extracted to establish a baseline record. Audio is transcribed with automatic speech recognition, and speaker diarization labels who spoke when, which is essential for multi-party calls. Video is often processed by sampling frames, running object or face detection, and applying optical character recognition to on-screen text. Reviewers then search the transcripts and metadata for keywords, concepts, or voices, and they can redact sensitive content before producing the media with a load file that links each clip to its transcript.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk around audio and video evidence include privacy laws, consent requirements for recording, and the need to preserve attorney-client privilege. Provenance is maintained through hash values, audit trails, and careful documentation of every transfer, because authentication challenges are common when media is edited or synthesized. Deepfakes and AI-generated audio raise new questions about authenticity, and this site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, which shows that rights disputes over media are already active. Handling these files also requires attention to data protection rules and to the risk of spoliation if evidence is not preserved.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The volume of audio and video evidence continues to grow, and review tools are moving toward more automated transcription, translation, and redaction. Provenance standards such as C2PA aim to attach verifiable origin data to media, which could help with authentication in court. Regulation is expanding, with 6979 state AI bills tracked on this site, and some of these may address synthetic media and evidence handling. The direction is toward faster, more accurate processing that still keeps a human reviewer in the loop for judgment calls.
